The Golden redhorse (Moxostoma erythrurum) is a mid-sized catostomid inhabiting warmwater streams and rivers across the central and eastern United States. During spawning, which occurs in late spring when water temperatures approach 18 °C [T = 18 °C], females release adhesive demersal eggs over gravel substrate. The fertilised ovum measures approximately 2.4 millimetres in diameter, and the resulting yolk-sac larva emerges with a minimal wet weight at birth of 0.0072 grams [Wwb = 0.0072 grams]. This initial mass is characteristic of catostomid larvae that depend entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days of exogenous feeding transition. First feeding commences shortly after yolk-sac resorption, and the planktonic larva grows rapidly through the summer months. Under controlled laboratory conditions, the egg diameter and larval weight at emergence have been confirmed to follow predictive relationships common within the genus. The fine sediments and moderate current velocities typical of spawning riffles likely aid in protecting the incubating eggs, and this habitat selection is consistent with spawning behaviors observed in related Moxostoma species across the Mississippi River basin.

Juvenile Golden redhorse undergo a gradual metamorphosis as they transition from planktonic pelagic larvae to benthic, stream-dwelling juveniles capable of foraging on aquatic insect larvae. During this period, growth is strongly influenced by water temperature and food availability. Puberty is attained once individuals reach 35 centimeters [Lp = 35 centimeters] in total length, a threshold that typically occurs between the second and third year of life depending on local thermal regimes and resource abundance. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 458 grams [Wwp = approximately 458 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial somatic investment required before gonadal maturation can commence. At the onset of puberty, vitellogenesis begins in females and spermiation in males, marking the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Field surveys have indicated that size at maturity can vary modestly across the species' range, with individuals in more productive systems reaching puberty at slightly smaller sizes due to faster early growth. This variability underscores the importance of local environmental conditions in shaping life-history schedules within Moxostoma erythrurum.

The maximum lifespan of Golden redhorse has been estimated from scale and otolith annuli, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 4015 days [am = approximately 4015 days] under natural stream conditions at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This longevity, expressed as roughly 11 years [am = roughly 11 years], is typical of moderate-sized catostomids that exhibit an iteroparous reproductive strategy at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. An individual achieving this advanced age would have experienced numerous spawning seasons, with each successive year contributing to the cumulative reproductive output of the population. Long-term mark-recapture studies have shown that mortality rates increase gradually after the onset of senescence, but some adults persist well beyond the age of first reproduction. The extended lifespan is thought to be an adaptation to variable juvenile recruitment success in unpredictable lotic environments. Comparative analyses with congeners suggest that Moxostoma erythrurum is longer-lived than several smaller-bodied Moxostoma species but shorter-lived than the largest members of the genus, such as Moxostoma duquesnii, which can exceed 15 years in age.

Fecundity in Golden redhorse is high relative to body size, reflecting the species' reliance on a broadcast spawning strategy with no parental care. A single reproductively viable organism with an ultimate total length of 78 centimeters [Li = 78 centimeters] achieves an ultimate wet weight of approximately 4990 grams [Wwi = approximately 4990 grams], and at this size, females produce approximately 227,738 oocytes per year [Ri = approximately 227,738 oocytes per year] at 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This annual reproductive schedule is typical of temperate riverine catostomids. The high annual fecundity offsets the relatively high mortality experienced by eggs and larvae, ensuring that enough offspring survive to recruit into the juvenile stage. Egg surveys conducted over multiple spawning seasons have confirmed that peak reproductive activity is tightly synchronized with the seasonal thermal regime.

The asymptotic body size of 78 centimeters [Li = 78 centimeters] reported for Moxostoma erythrurum from in-stream surveys represents one of the larger values among the riverine Moxostoma species of North America. At this length, the ultimate wet weight of 4990 grams [Wwi = 4990 grams] is consistent with the species' robust, deep-bodied morphology. Comparing this species to its congener Moxostoma carinatum, which attains an adult body mass of approximately 3500 grams, the Golden redhorse is substantially heavier at its maximum size, likely reflecting differences in habitat productivity and diet composition. The life-history strategy of Moxostoma erythrurum is characterized by moderate growth rates, delayed maturity until a total length of 35 centimeters [Lp = 35 centimeters] is reached, and a relatively long potential lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years] at the thermal optimum of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This suite of traits positions the species as a moderately K-selected catostomid relative to smaller, shorter-lived cyprinids that share its riverine habitats. Future studies should examine how ongoing thermal alterations to stream environments may impact these life-history parameters.
